bib.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System

question: How can tree boosting be built as an end-to-end system that scales to billions of examples with few resources?
hypothesis: Algorithmic (sparsity-aware splits, weighted quantile sketch) and systems (cache-aware, out-of-core blocks) optimisations together yield state-of-the-art accuracy and large speedups.
contributions: A highly scalable end-to-end tree boosting system
A theoretically justified weighted quantile sketch for efficient proposal calculation
A novel sparsity-aware algorithm for parallel tree learning
An effective cache-aware block structure for out-of-core tree learning

method.summary: Gradient tree boosting with a regularised second-order objective, exact greedy and approximate (global/local, weighted quantile sketch) split finding, sparsity-aware default directions, and a column-block data layout with cache-aware prefetching, block compression and sharding for out-of-core and distributed training. Evaluated mainly on speed against scikit-learn, R gbm, pGBRT, Spark MLLib and H2O.

training.objective: L = sum l(yhat,y) + sum Omega(f_k), Omega = gamma T + 1/2 lambda ||w||^2, second-order Taylor approximation

results.claim: Second-order regularised objective gives optimal leaf weight w*_j = -(sum g_i)/(sum h_i + lambda) and split gain Eq 7 with penalty gamma per leaf.

limits: Experiments report speed and a few AUC/NDCG values from single runs with no variance.
Baseline comparisons use default-ish configs not described; scikit-learn is single-threaded per Table 1 while XGBoost used all cores.
Colsample explanations (few important features in Higgs; overfitting in LTRC) are untested conjectures.
Lambda, gamma and pGBRT/scikit-learn settings are not stated.
Sparsity-aware algorithm is not compared against imputation for accuracy.
